questions.question: What is glycerine and what is its use in microtechnique? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is glycerine and what is its use in microtechnique? [U/CO1]
  • Glycerine is a colourless, viscous, hygroscopic trihydric alcohol (1 mark). Use: serves as a temporary
  • mounting medium, prevents drying of sections, softens and clears tissues. ( 1 mark).

questions.question: List out the difference between sledge and rotary microtome. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Difference between sledge and rotary microtome. [K/CO1]
  • Sledge microtome: The knife moves over a fixed specimen. Used for hard or woody material and gives
  • thick sections. Rotary microtome: the knife is fixed and the specimen block moves up and down by a
  • rotating hand-wheel; used for paraffin-embedded material and gives thin serial sections/ribbons.

questions.question: Define the smear technique used in plant cytological studies. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Define the smear technique in plant cytological studies. [K/CO1]
  • A technique in which cells are spread as a thin film on a slide by gentle pressing or spreading.

questions.question: Define maceration in plant microtechnique. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Define maceration in plant microtechnique. [K/CO1]
  • Maceration is the process of separating the cells of a tissue by dissolving the middle lamella with chemicals
  • (e.g. Schultze's method, Jeffrey's method) so that individual cells such as vessels, tracheids and fibres can
  • be studied.

questions.question: What is meant by chamber volume in haemocytometer counting? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by Chamber volume in haemocytometer counting. [K/CO4]
  • Liberal valuation

  • Volume calculation- For a standard 1 mm² large square: 1 mm² × 0.1 mm = 0.1 mm³ (0.1 μL).

questions.question: Explain the preparation and use of safranin in plant microtechnique. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the preparation and use of safranin in plant microtechnique. [U/CO1]
  • Liberal valuation
  • In syllabus, it’s mentioned to study only the composition. Preparation:
  • • Stock solution- Add 2.5 g safranin-O to 100.0 ml 95% ethyl alcohol.
  • • Working solution -Add 10.0 ml safranin and ethyl alcohol solution made in step 1 to 90.0 ml
  • distilled water. (2.5 marks).
  • Use: stains lignified, suberised and cutinised walls (xylem, sclerenchyma), nuclei and chromosomes red;
  • commonly used with fast green/light green as counterstain in double staining of sections (2.5 marks).

questions.question: Explain the working of a compound light microscope. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Working of a compound light microscope. [U/CO3]
  • • Parts: mechanical (base, arm, stage, body tube, nosepiece, focusing knobs) and optical (light
  • source/mirror, condenser and diaphragm, objectives, eyepiece).
  • • Working: light is focused by the condenser on the specimen; the objective forms a real, inverted,
  • magnified primary image; the eyepiece further magnifies it to a virtual image. Total
  • magnification = objective × eyepiece power.

questions.question: Explain the principle and working of a spectrophotometer. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the Principle and working of a spectrophotometer. [U/CO2]
  • • Principle (2 marks): Beer–Lambert law; absorbance is proportional to concentration and path
  • length.
  • • Working (2.5 marks): monochromatic light passes through the blank and then the sample; the
  • detector measures transmitted light, converted to absorbance; concentration is read from a
  • standard curve.

questions.question: Describe the process of image formation in SEM. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the process of Image formation in SEM. [U/CO3]
  • • Electron gun produces a beam (tungsten filament/FEG, 1–30 kV), focused by condenser and
  • objective lenses under high vacuum.
  • • Scanning the specimen-Special scanning coils sweep the probe back and forth across the coated
  • specimen surface.
  • • Beam–specimen interaction yields secondary electrons (topography), backscattered electrons
  • (composition) and X-rays.
  • • The detector collects the signal, which is amplified and synchronised with the scan to build the
  • image on a monitor.
  • • Sample preparation (optional): fixation, dehydration, critical point drying, gold sputter coating.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the principle and applications of ultracentrifugation. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the Principle and applications of ultracentrifugation. [U/CO2]
  • • Principle: separation of particles by sedimentation under very high centrifugal force (up to about
  • 10⁶ × g, above 60,000 rpm) in a refrigerated vacuum chamber; rate depends on size, shape,
  • density (sedimentation coefficient, Svedberg unit S); RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × rpm².
  • • Applications: isolation of organelles, ribosomes, viruses; purification of DNA/plasmids and
  • proteins; determination of molecular weight and density, etc.

questions.question: Describe how the electric charge of a molecule affects electrophoretic mobility. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• How the electric charge of a molecule affects electrophoretic mobility. [U/CO2]
  • • A molecule moves in an electric field because it has an electrical charge.
  • • The greater its net charge, the more strongly it is attracted towards the oppositely charged
  • electrode and the faster it moves.
  • • positively charged molecules move to the cathode and negatively charged ones to the anode
  • • Net charge of a molecule depends on its chemical groups, and the pH of the surrounding buffer

questions.question: Briefly explain the working and application of paper chromatography. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Briefly explain the working and application of paper chromatography. [U/CO3]
  • Working:
  • • Put a small spot of the sample on the bottom of the paper, and let it dry.
  • • Hang the Whatman filter paper (Stationary phase) in a closed chamber with the lower edge
  • dipping in the solvent (mobile phase), (below the spot).
  • • The solvent rises by capillary action and carries the compounds with it. Compounds that dissolve
  • better in the solvent move faster and further.
  • • Remove the paper when the solvent front nears the top and mark the front. Dry the paper.
  • • Calculate Rf = distance travelled by the compound ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front.
  • Applications - Separation and identification of amino acids and sugars, Separation of plant pigments such
  • as chlorophylls and carotenoids, Analysis of flavonoids, organic acids and other plant metabolites,
  • Checking the purity of a compound

questions.question: Compare and contrast HPLC and column chromatography. / [CO5] [5x8 = 40]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare and contrast HPLC and column chromatography. [U/CO5]
  • Award 5 marks for a comparison covering at least five points, plus similarities.
  • Feature Column chromatography HPLC
  • Stationary phase Packed column Fine packed column
  • Driving Force Gravity flow High pressure pump
  • Particle size Large (60–200 µm) Small (3–10 µm)
  • Resolution Low High
  • Detection Manual fractions, offline Online detectors (UV, PDA, RI, fluorescence)
  • Sample amount Large Small
  • Scale preparative analytical or preparative
  • Speed Slow Fast
  • Cost Low High (pump, column, detector)
  • Similarity: both use a stationary and a mobile phase and separate by differential adsorption/partition (1
  • mark).

questions.question: Distinguish between temporary and permanent slide preparation techniques. Discuss the steps involved and suitable mounting media for each. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Distinguish between temporary and permanent slide preparation techniques. Discuss the steps
  • involved and suitable mounting media for each. [U/CO1]
  • • Distinction (3 marks): temporary slides are quick, last only a short time, mounted in water/glycerine ;
  • permanent slides are made from fixed, processed material, stored for years, mounted in a resinous
  • medium. (Include at least three points of difference.)
  • • Steps in temporary preparation (2 marks): select material, cut thin freehand section, stain
  • (safranin/toluidine blue, iodine), mount in water or dilute glycerine.
  • • Steps in permanent preparation (3 marks): killing and fixing (FAA), dehydration (graded alcohol series),
  • clearing (xylene), embedding in paraffin wax, sectioning (rotary microtome), staining (e.g. safranin–fast
  • green), mounting
  • • Mounting media (2 marks): temporary: water, dilute glycerine, lactophenol; semi-permanent: glycerine
  • jelly; permanent: Canada balsam (RI about 1.52), DPX, Euparal.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the working and applications of colorimeter. / [CO3] [10x1 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the working and applications of colorimeter. [U/CO3]
  • • Components (3 marks): light source (tungsten lamp), filter (selects wavelength range), cuvette holding
  • the sample, photocell/photodetector, galvanometer or digital display.
  • • Working (3 marks): zero with blank, select filter (complementary colour), read absorbance of
  • standards, plot a standard curve, read concentration of the unknown.
  • • Applications (4 marks): Quantitative estimation of coloured substances in solution. Measurement of
  • microbial growth, Testing water quality/ soil nutrients etc., Estimation of biomolecules such as
  • proteins and carbohydrates, Estimation of pigments and other biological compounds.(Any 4)
